chapter_summary:
Every device connected to a network is a potential target for attackers. Raspberry Pi projects are no exception. A Pi running a web server, MQTT broker, or cloud client can be exploited if it is not properly secured. Security should be considered from the beginning, not added as an afterthought.

The first step is to change default credentials and use strong passwords. If you still have an old image with the default `pi` user, create a new user and delete the default account. Use a password manager to generate unique passwords.

For SSH, key-based authentication is much more secure than passwords. To set it up, generate an SSH key pair on your main computer:

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"
```

Copy the public key to the Pi:

```bash
ssh-copy-id alex@raspberrypi.local
```

Then disable password authentication by editing `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`:

```bash
PasswordAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin no
```

Restart the SSH service:

```bash
sudo systemctl restart ssh
```

A firewall controls which network traffic is allowed. The `ufw` firewall is easy to use on Raspberry Pi OS:

```bash
sudo apt install ufw
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp      # SSH
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp      # HTTP
sudo ufw allow 1883/tcp    # MQTT
sudo ufw enable
```

Only open ports that you actually need. If you do not need SSH from the internet, do not expose port 22 externally.

Keep the system updated:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade
```

Disable services you do not use. If your project does not need Bluetooth, consider disabling it. If you do not need the graphical desktop, use Raspberry Pi OS Lite to reduce the attack surface.

Finally, follow the principle of least privilege. Run services as a non-root user whenever possible. Do not store sensitive data in plain text. Use HTTPS for web interfaces. Monitor logs with `journalctl` to detect unusual activity.

screens.title: IoT Security and Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Protect your Raspberry Pi: credentials, SSH keys, firewall basics, and minimal attack surface

narration.text: Every networked device is a potential target, and a Raspberry Pi with a web server, MQTT broker, or cloud client is no exception. In this lesson you will learn practical steps to harden a Pi from first boot to ongoing maintenance. We begin with simple but critical moves: replacing default users, using strong unique passwords, and switching SSH to key-based authentication. Then we cover network controls using ufw to allow only needed ports, how to keep the OS and packages patched, and why disabling unused services reduces risk. You will see concrete command examples you can run on your Pi and a short hands-on checklist to practice. A common misconception is that a Pi is too small or obscure to be attacked; in reality, insecure devices are often the easiest targets. By applying these small, repeatable controls you drastically reduce exposure and make a device resilient. Notice the three key topics listed below: credential hygiene, SSH keys and firewall configuration. As you move forward, ask yourself which network services your project actually needs and how you can run them with the least privilege. That question is the practical core of this chapter.

keyIdea.title: Big picture
keyIdea.text: Security is layered: credentials, network controls, minimal services, updates, and least privilege together reduce risk.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this lesson

narration.text: By the end of this lesson you will identify common security risks for Raspberry Pi projects, and you will be able to take four core actions to protect a device. First, you will learn to remove default users and enforce strong, unique credentials using a password manager. Second, you will secure remote administration by creating and installing an SSH key pair and disabling password-based login. Third, you will configure the ufw firewall to expose only required ports and verify its status. Fourth, you will adopt maintenance practices: keep the system updated, disable services you do not need, and run services with the least privilege. Each objective maps to a practical milestone: creating a new user and deleting the default account, successfully logging in with a key and confirming password login is disabled, installing and enabling ufw with precise allow rules, and running updates safely. These skills matter because they turn a one-off hobby device into a manageable, auditable system. We'll provide short checks so you can verify each milestone on your Pi. Think about which services your project truly needs before allowing network access; that decision guides all the steps you will take.

screens.title: Why secure a Raspberry Pi?
screens.subtitle: Threat model and practical risk understanding

narration.text: Securing a Raspberry Pi begins with a clear threat model: anything exposed to a network can be discovered and probed. For many projects the risk is not a targeted nation-state attack but automated scanners and opportunistic attackers who seek devices with default credentials or open services. Understanding that threat helps you choose controls that are proportionate: change default users and passwords, limit exposed network ports, and run only the services you need. For example, a Pi running a small web interface but left with the default account becomes an automated target for scripts that try common usernames and passwords; this is how many compromises happen. A common misconception is that low-cost hobby devices are unlikely targets. In practice, attackers prefer easy wins, and insecure Pis provide those. The practical takeaway is to apply basic hygiene immediately: create a unique user, remove defaults, and avoid exposing unnecessary services. That combination changes your device from a high-risk entry point to a manageable endpoint. As you proceed in the lesson, carry a simple checklist: credentials, SSH keys, firewall, updates, and least privilege. Which single step will you run first on your Pi?

keyIdea.title: Threat model
keyIdea.text: Automated scans and opportunistic attackers target default credentials and exposed services; basic hygiene closes the largest risks.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Why secure a Raspberry Pi?
Definition
A threat model identifies who might attack your device, how they would discover it, and what they aim to do. For many Pis the likely attackers are automated scanners seeking default credentials or open ports.
Concrete example
A Pi with the 'pi' user and password left in place can be found by automated scripts and accessed without effort. Removing the default user prevents that immediate entry vector.
Key takeaway
Basic hygiene reduces the largest risks quickly. You do not need perfect security, but you do need to remove obvious, automated attack paths.
Common mistakes and checks
  • Keeping default usernames or weak passwords.
  • Exposing SSH to the public internet without keys or rate limiting.
  • Running many unnecessary services that increase the attack surface.
Try this
Before connecting a Pi to the internet, create your non-default user and confirm you can log in as that user.

screens.title: Change default user and enforce strong credentials
screens.subtitle: Create a new user, remove 'pi', and use a password manager

narration.text: The first practical control is credential hygiene. Start by creating a new user account on the Pi and granting it appropriate sudo privileges, then delete the default 'pi' user. Doing this removes a predictable account attackers try first. Use a password manager to generate and store a unique, strong password for your new account rather than reusing passwords. A simple process: create the new user, test login and sudo access, copy any needed configuration or SSH keys to the new account, and finally remove the default account. For example, after creating user 'alex', confirm you can switch to that user and run sudo commands before deleting 'pi'. A common mistake is removing the old account before verifying the new account works, which can lock you out. Another misconception is that password-only defenses are sufficient; they are not. Passwords are necessary but should be combined with key-based SSH and minimal exposure. The practical takeaway: always verify access with the new user before removing the default, and prefer generated passwords stored in a manager to avoid reuse and weak credentials. Change default user and enforce strong credentials means create and verify a new user, use a password manager for unique passwords, then remove the default account only after testing access.. In practical terms, create a new user, remove 'pi', and use a password manager. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Credential hygiene
keyIdea.text: Create and verify a new user, use a password manager for unique passwords, then remove the default account only after testing access.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Change default user
Step-by-step
  1. Create a new user and set a strong password.
  2. Grant sudo if needed and confirm sudo works.
  3. Move SSH keys or configs to the new user.
  4. Delete the old 'pi' account only after verification.
Concrete example
Create user 'alex', test login and sudo, then delete 'pi' to prevent automated login attempts using that account.
Common mistake
Deleting the default user before confirming the new account works. Always verify access first to avoid lockout.
Pro tip
Use a password manager to create unique passwords and avoid reuse across devices and services.
Key Takeaway

Replace default accounts immediately and verify new account access before removal to close the most basic attack vector.

screens.title: SSH key-based authentication
screens.subtitle: Generate keys, install the public key, and why it is safer than passwords

narration.text: SSH key-based authentication replaces password login with a cryptographic key pair: a private key you keep on your computer and a public key placed on the Pi. Generate an ed25519 key pair on your main computer with the standard command shown in this chapter. This algorithm produces small keys with strong security, and because authentication uses the private key rather than a password, it effectively prevents brute-force guessing and password harvesting. After generating keys, copy the public key to the Pi using the provided copy command. Then edit the SSH server configuration to disable password authentication and prevent root login. A practical example: generate the key, copy the public key for user 'alex' on the Pi, test that you can log in via the key, then change PasswordAuthentication to no and restart SSH. A common misconception is that disabling password login will lock you out; you must test the key login before making that change. The takeaway is that key-based authentication reduces the likelihood of successful automated attacks and is a necessary step for any Pi connected beyond a trusted LAN.

keyIdea.title: Key benefits
keyIdea.text: Key-based SSH prevents password guessing and automated brute-force attacks; always test key login before disabling passwords.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › SSH key-based authentication
Commands to run
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"
ssh-copy-id alex@raspberrypi.local
Generate the key locally, then copy the public key to the Pi for the target user. Test login using your SSH client; it should use the private key automatically.
Edit SSH server
# in /etc/ssh/sshd_config
PasswordAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin no
After confirming key login works, change these settings and restart SSH with the command shown in the chapter to apply the change.
Misconception check
Do not disable password authentication until you can log in with the key. Otherwise you risk locking yourself out of the device.
Key Takeaway
Use ed25519 keys, install the public key on the Pi, verify key login, then disable password-based SSH to prevent brute-force attacks.

screens.title: Secure SSH configuration and safe restart
screens.subtitle: Edit sshd_config and restart SSH safely

narration.text: Securing SSH has two steps: configuration and safe application of that configuration. The chapter shows the key configuration directives to change: set PasswordAuthentication no and PermitRootLogin no in the server configuration file. But the operational lesson is about doing this without losing access. After you edit the file, restart the SSH service using the recommended systemctl command. Before restarting, open a second SSH session so you keep a working connection while testing the new settings. This reduces the risk of being locked out. For a concrete walkthrough: open a second terminal and ssh into the Pi as your new user; make the configuration change; restart SSH; if the new session still works, you can close the old one. A common mistake is editing the config, restarting, and then discovering the key wasn't installed correctly. Always confirm key-based login first. The practical takeaway is that secure configuration must be validated with an independent session, and using systemctl to restart the service provides a clear, reversible operation if you planned for validation. Secure SSH configuration and safe restart means edit sshd_config to disable passwords and root login, but always validate with a second session before closing your working connection.. In practical terms, edit sshd_config and restart ssh safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safe change
keyIdea.text: Edit sshd_config to disable passwords and root login, but always validate with a second session before closing your working connection.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Secure SSH configuration
Configuration
PasswordAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin no
Place these lines in /etc/ssh/sshd_config and save the file. They prevent password logins and root remote sign-in.
Safe restart
sudo systemctl restart ssh
Open a second SSH session before restarting so you retain a recovery connection. Only close the old session after the new login is confirmed.
Checklist before restart
  • Confirm public key exists in authorized_keys for your user.
  • Open a second SSH session to the Pi.
  • Apply config change and restart SSH, then verify new session works.

screens.title: Firewall basics with ufw
screens.subtitle: Install ufw, add allow rules, and enable the firewall

narration.text: A firewall controls which network traffic reaches your device. On Raspberry Pi OS the uncomplicated firewall utility, ufw, provides a simple interface to allow or deny ports. The practical commands shown in the chapter install ufw, add rules for necessary ports like SSH, HTTP, or MQTT, and enable the firewall. For example, run the install command, then allow 22/tcp for SSH, 80/tcp for HTTP, and 1883/tcp for MQTT if your project uses that protocol. Finally, enable ufw to enforce the rules. The security principle is to open only what you need; unnecessary open ports increase exposure. A common misconception is that a firewall will keep out any threat; a firewall limits exposure but does not replace secure configurations or updates. Another common mistake is allowing SSH from everywhere when you only need it on a private network; consider restricting access to known hosts when possible. The takeaway is that ufw is a small, effective control for most Pi projects and should be part of the standard setup before exposing a device to wider networks. Firewall basics with ufw means use ufw to expose only required ports; it reduces attack surface but complements, not replaces, other security practices.. In practical terms, install ufw, add allow rules, and enable the firewall. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: UFW role
keyIdea.text: Use ufw to expose only required ports; it reduces attack surface but complements, not replaces, other security practices.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Firewall with ufw
Install and allow commands
sudo apt install ufw
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp # SSH
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp # HTTP
sudo ufw allow 1883/tcp # MQTT
sudo ufw enable
Run only rules you need. After enabling, verify active rules with the status command provided in the chapter.
Practical guidance
  • Only open ports required by the project.
  • Avoid exposing SSH publicly when not needed.
  • Consider restricting rules to known IPs where possible.
Key Takeaway

UFW is a lightweight control to enforce which ports are reachable; use it to minimize network exposure before publishing services.

screens.title: Open ports: what to allow and what to avoid
screens.subtitle: Decide which services truly need network access

narration.text: When configuring network access for a Pi, be selective. The chapter lists common service ports you might consider: 22 for SSH, 80 for HTTP, and 1883 for MQTT. Allow ports only when the service is required and properly secured. For instance, allow 22/tcp for SSH when you need remote administration, but prefer key-based authentication and limit access to trusted networks. If your project only serves a local web dashboard, consider restricting HTTP access to the LAN rather than exposing port 80 to the internet. A typical mistake is opening many convenience services for development and forgetting to remove them before deployment. Another contrast: a device that exposes an MQTT broker widely without authentication can become a channel for attackers to publish or subscribe to messages, while a broker bound to the LAN and using authentication is far safer. The practical rule of thumb is least exposure: if you don't need it open, close it. That decision reduces the number of attack vectors you must defend. Open ports: what to allow and what to avoid means only allow ports and services your project requires. prefer lan-only access and authenticated services over public exposure.. In practical terms, decide which services truly need network access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Least exposure
keyIdea.text: Only allow ports and services your project requires. Prefer LAN-only access and authenticated services over public exposure.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Open ports: allow vs avoid
Common allows
22/tcp — SSH for remote admin (use keys). 80/tcp — HTTP if you host a web server. 1883/tcp — MQTT broker for IoT messaging (secure with auth).
Example decision
If you only access a dashboard on your local home network, do not open port 80 to the public internet. Keep it LAN-only.
Risk comparison
Publicly exposed services need stronger controls: authentication, encryption, and monitoring. LAN-only services still require authentication, but exposure is reduced.
Common mistake
Leaving development ports open after testing. Always re-check firewall rules before deployment.
Key Takeaway
Use the principle: if you do not need a port open, do not allow it. That single rule eliminates many common exposures.

screens.title: Keep software updated
screens.subtitle: Use apt update and upgrade regularly and understand why updates matter

narration.text: Keeping the operating system and installed packages up to date is one of the simplest and most effective defenses. The chapter gives the exact commands: sudo apt update to refresh package lists, and sudo apt upgrade to install updates. Updates often include security fixes for services that could be exploited if left unpatched. For an example routine, run these commands weekly or more frequently for devices connected to wider networks. A misconception is that updates are optional for hobby devices. In reality, unpatched systems accumulate known vulnerabilities over time, increasing risk. Another operational note: review upgrade notes when large upgrades are available to ensure your services will still run after the update. If your Pi runs critical services, schedule updates during maintenance windows and test in a staging environment when possible. The takeaway is to make updates a routine part of your device life cycle so you are not left vulnerable to defects that have already been fixed upstream. Keep software updated means run apt update and apt upgrade regularly; treat updates as maintenance to reduce exposure from known vulnerabilities.. In practical terms, use apt update and upgrade regularly and understand why updates matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Routine updates
keyIdea.text: Run apt update and apt upgrade regularly; treat updates as maintenance to reduce exposure from known vulnerabilities.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Keep software updated
Update commands
sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade
Run updates regularly and review any notes before applying large upgrades. For critical devices, test updates in a separate environment first.
Why it matters
Updates patch known vulnerabilities. An unpatched package is a known route attackers can exploit; routine updates close those routes.
Key Takeaway

Make updates a scheduled task so security fixes are applied promptly and your device remains protected against known issues.

screens.title: Disable unnecessary services
screens.subtitle: Reduce attack surface by removing or disabling unused components

narration.text: Every running service increases the device's attack surface. The chapter recommends disabling services you do not use, such as Bluetooth or the graphical desktop, by choosing lighter system images or stopping units you don't need. For example, if your project is a headless sensor, using Raspberry Pi OS Lite avoids installing the desktop environment and related services that could be exploited. Similarly, disable Bluetooth if your project doesn't use it. The concrete steps depend on the service: use systemctl to stop and disable services, and uninstall packages that are unnecessary. A common misconception is that leaving extras installed is harmless; however, installed but unused services can still provide vulnerabilities and maintenance burden. The practical takeaway is to minimize software footprint: fewer packages and services mean fewer update obligations and fewer potential vulnerabilities to monitor. Before disabling anything, verify the service is not required by your project to avoid breaking functionality. Disable unnecessary services means remove or disable services not required by your project to lower maintenance and reduce potential vulnerabilities.. In practical terms, reduce attack surface by removing or disabling unused components. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Minimal footprint
keyIdea.text: Remove or disable services not required by your project to lower maintenance and reduce potential vulnerabilities.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Disable unnecessary services
Why minimize services?
Each service can contain bugs and require updates. Removing what you do not use reduces the number of components to secure and monitor.
Example
Choose Raspberry Pi OS Lite for headless projects to avoid desktop packages and services you do not need.
How to disable
Use systemctl stop and systemctl disable for services, and remove packages with apt when not needed. Always test functionality after disabling.
Common mistake
Disabling services without checking dependencies. Verify that removing one service does not break another required by your project.

screens.title: Principle of least privilege and HTTPS
screens.subtitle: Run services as non-root and secure web interfaces with TLS

narration.text: Least privilege means running processes with the minimum permissions they require. For Raspberry Pi projects, this often translates to running daemons as a dedicated non-root user and avoiding storing secrets in plain text files. For web interfaces, use HTTPS to protect credentials and data in transit. The chapter highlights running services as non-root and avoiding storing sensitive data unencrypted. For a concrete example, run a lightweight web server as an unprivileged user and secure it with TLS when exposed beyond the local network. A common misconception is that running as root is simpler and fine for small projects; however, root privileges amplify the impact of any compromise. The practical takeaway is to separate privileges: create service accounts with only the needed permissions, store secrets in protected files, and prefer encrypted channels for any remote or web access. Monitoring logs with journalctl helps detect unusual activity, which is another important complement to least privilege. Principle of least privilege and HTTPS means run services as non-root, secure web interfaces with https, and protect sensitive data to limit the impact of a compromise.. In practical terms, run services as non-root and secure web interfaces with tls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Least privilege
keyIdea.text: Run services as non-root, secure web interfaces with HTTPS, and protect sensitive data to limit the impact of a compromise.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Least privilege & HTTPS
Least privilege
Create dedicated service users and avoid running network services as root. This limits what an attacker can do if a service is compromised.
Monitoring
Use journalctl to review logs for unusual activity and to help detect potential compromises early.
HTTPS for web interfaces
Use TLS for any web interface exposed beyond a trusted LAN so credentials and data are encrypted in transit.
Key Takeaway

Least privilege and encrypted channels reduce both the chance of compromise and its potential impact.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: SSH keys and ufw checklist
screens.subtitle: A short lab to practice the core steps and verify results

narration.text: The chapter includes a concise hands-on activity you can run on your Pi. The lab covers three objectives: set up SSH key-based authentication, disable password login, and configure ufw to allow only SSH and HTTP. Follow the exact sequence: generate an ed25519 key on your computer, copy the public key to the Pi for your user, and verify you can log in using the key. Next, edit the SSH server configuration to set PasswordAuthentication no and PermitRootLogin no; open a second SSH session before restarting the service to avoid lockout, then restart ssh with systemctl. Finally, install ufw, add rules for 22/tcp and 80/tcp if you need them, and enable ufw. Confirm the firewall rules with the status command. A common mistake is enabling the firewall before ensuring you have an open rule for SSH and a working key—this can cut off access. The takeaway: follow the sequence carefully and verify each step so the device remains accessible while becoming more secure. Hands-on activity: SSH keys and ufw checklist means generate keys, copy the public key, disable password auth after testing, install and enable ufw with allow rules, and verify status.. In practical terms, a short lab to practice the core steps and verify results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lab checklist
keyIdea.text: Generate keys, copy the public key, disable password auth after testing, install and enable ufw with allow rules, and verify status.

Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Hands-on activity
Activity steps
  1. Generate keys: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com".
  2. Copy public key: ssh-copy-id alex@raspberrypi.local and test key login.
  3. Edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config to set PasswordAuthentication no and PermitRootLogin no, open a second session then sudo systemctl restart ssh.
  4. Install ufw, allow 22/tcp and 80/tcp if needed, enable ufw and run status to confirm.

Enabling the firewall without ensuring SSH key access and an allow rule first, which can lock you out.

screens.title: What to Remember — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Three essential concepts from this chapter

narration.text: Here are three compact concepts to carry forward. First, strong credentials and removing default users block the simplest automated attacks; create a new user, use a password manager, and delete 'pi' after verification. Second, SSH key-based authentication is significantly stronger than passwords; generate an ed25519 key pair, install the public key on the Pi, and only then disable password authentication. Third, a firewall like ufw limits network exposure; allow only the ports your project needs and verify the rules after enabling. Each of these concepts is practical and actionable, and together they form the foundation of a secure Pi configuration. As a quick reflection, ask yourself which of these three items you have not yet applied to your device and start with that one. These habits reduce the most common risks quickly and should be part of your standard setup process.

keyIdea.title: Essentials
keyIdea.text: Credentials, SSH keys, and firewall rules are the core, high-impact controls for Raspberry Pi security.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Key Concepts
Strong Credentials
Remove defaults and use unique passwords to block easy automated access.
SSH Key Auth
Use ed25519 keys and disable password authentication once key login is confirmed.
Firewall (ufw)
Allow only required ports and verify rules to reduce network exposure.
Summary

Start with these three controls to secure a Raspberry Pi quickly: credentials, keys, and firewall. They provide immediate, high-impact protection.

narration.text: Three more practical reminders close this chapter. First, keep the system and packages updated regularly using apt update and apt upgrade to apply security fixes. Second, disable or remove services you do not need to minimize the number of components that require maintenance and could be exploited. Third, run services with least privilege and use HTTPS for web interfaces so credentials and data are protected in transit. Together these practices complement credential and firewall work and make your Pi resilient over time. As a quick reflection, pick one maintenance habit—regular updates, service minimization, or privilege separation—and make it part of your next weekly routine. Small, consistent actions like these prevent the gradual accumulation of risk and keep projects safe as they grow. Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › What to Remember — Part 2
Keep Updated
Use apt update and apt upgrade regularly to apply security fixes to packages and the OS.
Disable Unused Services
Stop and remove packages and units you do not need to reduce attack surface and maintenance effort.
Least Privilege & HTTPS
Run services with minimal permissions and use TLS for web interfaces to protect data in transit.
Final takeaway

Security is an ongoing practice: apply the basics now, then maintain them with routine updates and attention to services and privileges.
